title: The Preprocessor & Macros
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand that macros are blind text substitution—precedence bugs, double-eval, and header-guard mistakes are classic C screening traps.

phases.goal: Establish that the preprocessor is a pure text engine that rewrites source before the compiler sees it.

must_hit.point: The preprocessor is a pure text-substitution engine; it knows nothing about C data types, variables, loops, or scope, and a macro error is a text replacement error, not a type error.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says macros rewrite tokens before compilation and do not understand C semantics.

must_hit.point: #include pastes another file's contents at the directive site; <filename.h> searches system directories, while "filename.h" searches the current source directory first then falls back to system directories.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts angle-bracket system/library includes with quoted project-header includes.

must_hit.point: A header guard (#ifndef/#define/#endif) or #pragma once ensures a header's contents are pasted only once per translation unit, preventing duplicate struct/type definitions from diamond includes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains first include defines the guard macro and later includes skip the block until #endif.

must_hit.point: #define creates a macro that blindly substitutes replacement text; object-like macros map an identifier to a fixed token sequence (manifest constants), while function-like macros take arguments but substitute argument text rather than passing values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes object-like constants from function-like text replacement that looks like a call.

probes: What does the preprocessor do before the C compiler runs, and what does it not understand?
How do #include <...> and #include "..." differ, and why do headers need include guards?

hints.1: Think about what happens to your .c file before any type checking.
hints.2: Start from # directives: paste (#include) versus replace (#define), then where each include form searches.
hints.3: Preprocessor = text only → translation unit; <> system dirs, "" local then system; #ifndef MY_HEADER_H ... #endif so a diamond include does not redefine a struct.

phases.goal: Show how fragile macro expansion is fixed with parentheses, do-while(0), and the special token operators.

must_hit.point: A robust function-like macro must parenthesize every parameter use and the entire replacement list so argument expressions and surrounding operators cannot change precedence (e.g. DOUBLE_BAD(3 + 4) becoming 3 + 4 * 2).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate expands DOUBLE_BAD without parens to a precedence bug, then shows ((x) * 2) as the fix.

must_hit.point: Even with parentheses, a parameter appearing more than once in the replacement list causes multiple evaluation of the argument text—side effects like a++ or a function call run multiple times (the double-eval trap).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate expands SQUARE_SAFE(i++) to ((i++) * (i++)) and flags undefined/unintended behavior.

must_hit.point: Multi-statement macros must be wrapped in do { ... } while (0) so they act as one statement needing a trailing semicolon and stay safe inside brace-less if/else (otherwise a trailing exit can always execute).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows the LOG_ERROR if expansion where exit always runs, then the do-while(0) idiom.

must_hit.point: # stringizes a parameter into a string literal; ## token-pastes two tokens into one; variadic macros use ... and __VA_ARGS__; conditional compilation (#if/#ifdef/#ifndef/#elif/#else/#endif) and -D flags gate platforms, features, and debug vs release.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate can sketch PRINT_INT with #var, DECLARE_STRUCT with name##_data, DEBUG_PRINT(...), and an #ifdef _WIN32 branch.

probes: Walk through what DOUBLE_BAD(3 + 4) expands to and how you would write DOUBLE_SAFE.
Why wrap a multi-statement macro in do { ... } while (0), and what goes wrong with SQUARE_SAFE(i++)?

hints.1: Mentally paste the argument text into the macro body before thinking about C evaluation order.
hints.2: Cover three mechanics: parentheses for precedence, multiple appearances for double-eval, and do-while(0) for statement shape.
hints.3: #define DOUBLE_SAFE(x) ((x) * 2); SQUARE_SAFE(i++) → ((i++)*(i++)); LOG_ERROR without do-while(0) leaves exit(1) outside the if.

phases.goal: Decide when macros are justified versus const, enum, and inline.

must_hit.point: Modern C prefers native features over macros when possible because they give type safety, scope, and debugger visibility: use const or enum for values and inline functions instead of function-like macros.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defaults to const/enum/inline and names type checking and avoiding double-eval as reasons.

must_hit.point: Use macros only when you must manipulate text: stringizing (#), token-pasting (##), capturing __FILE__/__LINE__, do { ... } while (0) control-flow bundling, conditional compilation, or type-agnostic operations like container_of that cannot be ordinary functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists text-only jobs macros uniquely enable rather than treating macros as a general abstraction tool.

must_hit.point: #pragma once is a widely supported alternative to classic header guards: same purpose, less naming-collision risk, and can compile slightly faster.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate compares #ifndef guards to #pragma once without claiming #pragma once is in the C standard.

probes: When should you use a macro versus inline, const, or enum?
Would you pick a traditional include guard or #pragma once, and why?

hints.1: Ask what macros cannot give you that language features can.
hints.2: Separate value macros, function-like macros, and text-only needs (#, ##, __FILE__, conditional compilation).
hints.3: Prefer const/enum/inline; macros only for text manipulation and idioms like container_of; #pragma once ≈ guards with fewer name collisions.

phases.goal: Apply preprocessor idioms and spot production pitfalls in headers and macros.

must_hit.point: Headers must hold declarations only; putting function or variable definitions in a header included by multiple .c files yields multiple-definition linker errors.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates declarations in headers from definitions in .c files and names the link-time multiple-definition failure.

must_hit.point: ARRAY_SIZE(arr) is (sizeof(arr) / sizeof((arr)[0])); container_of recovers a containing struct pointer via offsetof—both are type-agnostic macro idioms used in systems code.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes the ARRAY_SIZE formula and explains container_of as ptr minus offsetof(member).

must_hit.point: assert from <assert.h> reports failure with __FILE__ and __LINE__; defining NDEBUG before including <assert.h> compiles asserts to nothing—and there is no standard C macro fix for double-eval, so use an inline function instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties assert to predefined macros/NDEBUG and recommends inline when side-effecting arguments are possible.

probes: What goes wrong if you put a function definition in a header included by two .c files?
Write ARRAY_SIZE and explain when you would still refuse a macro and use inline instead.

hints.1: Think link time for headers, and sizeof for array length.
hints.2: Declarations vs definitions across translation units; macros that must stay generic or capture source location.
hints.3: Multiple .c includes → multiple definitions at link; #define ARRAY_SIZE(a) (sizeof(a)/sizeof((a)[0])); side-effect args → inline, not a macro.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer const or enum for values and inline functions for callable logic (type safety, scope, debuggers, no double-eval). Reserve macros for text-only needs: #, ##, __FILE__/__LINE__, do-while(0) statement macros, conditional compilation, and idioms like container_of that cannot be ordinary functions.

Both prevent double inclusion per translation unit. Classic #ifndef/#define/#endif is portable standard practice; #pragma once is a widely supported extension with the same purpose, less naming-collision risk, and potentially slightly faster compiles.

Use <...> for system/standard/third-party headers searched in system directories; use "..." for project headers, which search the current source directory first and then fall back to system directories.

gotchas.trap: Function-like macro without parentheses (e.g. #define DOUBLE_BAD(x) x * 2 or #define SQUARE(x) x * x) so DOUBLE_BAD(3 + 4) or SQUARE(2 + 3) expands with wrong precedence.
gotchas.correction: Parenthesize every parameter use and the whole body: #define DOUBLE_SAFE(x) ((x) * 2); #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)).

gotchas.trap: Double-eval: passing a side-effecting argument into a macro that uses the parameter more than once (e.g. SQUARE_SAFE(i++) → ((i++) * (i++))).
gotchas.correction: No standard C macro fix; use an inline function so the argument is evaluated once with proper sequencing.

gotchas.trap: Multi-statement macro used in brace-less if, so only the first statement is conditional and later statements (e.g. exit(1)) always run.
gotchas.correction: Wrap the body in do { ... } while (0) so the macro is one statement that requires a trailing semicolon.

gotchas.trap: Putting function or variable definitions in a header included by multiple .c files.
gotchas.correction: Headers may contain only declarations (signatures, macros, structs, types); put definitions in a single .c to avoid multiple-definition linker errors.

gotchas.trap: Treating __func__ as a predefined macro like __FILE__ / __LINE__.
gotchas.correction: __func__ provides the current function name but is a predefined identifier, not a macro.
